title: Randomized Medicaid access increased one presidential-election turnout but not later turnout
source_unit: Low-income uninsured Oregon adults selected or not selected by the 2008 Medicaid lottery, linked to statewide voter records

observations.period: 2008 Oregon Medicaid lottery; November 2008 presidential election

denominator.unit: randomized lottery treatment-control voter-record contrast; published instrumental-variable estimate

medicaid_coverage_effect_on_turnout.unit: percentage points; approximately 7% relative to 34% control-group turnout

observations.method: Randomized selection in the Oregon Medicaid lottery used as an instrument for Medicaid coverage, linked to Oregon statewide voter registration and turnout records; analyses were prespecified.
observations.uncertainty: The estimate is local to low-income previously uninsured Oregon adults and the 2008 Medicaid expansion; the study cannot observe individual health, financial-relief, trust, attribution, or registration mechanisms directly. The registration increase is suggestive rather than statistically significant.
observations.subgroup: Lottery-eligible low-income uninsured adults ages 19–64; effects were concentrated among men and residents of Democratic counties.
observations.counterinterpretation: Coverage may have changed administrative access, health security, or eligibility-related contact rather than generalized political trust; the early turnout result may reflect new registration or election-specific mobilization.

denominator.unit: randomized lottery treatment-control voter-record contrasts across subsequent statewide, local, primary, and special elections

observations.method: Same Oregon Medicaid lottery design and statewide voter-record linkage as the 2008 turnout estimate.
observations.uncertainty: The experiment ended as a clean contrast after control-group members received a later opportunity to enter a new lottery; the follow-up does not establish durable political change beyond the observed election window.
observations.subgroup: Same lottery-eligible low-income uninsured Oregon adults.
observations.counterinterpretation: A short-lived turnout response can coexist with persistent coverage or financial effects; null later turnout does not rule out changes in other political actions, trust, or institutional use.

related_sources.claim: Published Quarterly Journal of Political Science article identifier
Official Oregon Health Insurance Experiment overview and results context

boundary: This record adds a randomized Medicaid-access-to-voter-participation route: coverage increased turnout in the November 2008 presidential election but not subsequent turnout through November 2010. It does not establish a causal trust effect, a universal Medicaid-to-voting effect, a specific household recovery mechanism, or durable political realignment.
